name: Security Engineer Roadmap
tagline: From how a packet and a certificate work to defending a system you did not build
summary: Security is applied systems knowledge, so this path deliberately starts with the things being attacked: code, the network, and the cryptography that protects traffic in transit. From there it moves through identity — who is calling and what they may do — then the application layer where most breaches actually happen, then the infrastructure and delivery pipeline that has become the favourite target, and ends with detection, response and a worked identity design.

steps.label: Programming fundamentals
steps.note: You cannot review, exploit or fix code you cannot read, and almost every vulnerability is ultimately a line of code that trusted its input.

steps.label: Linux, processes & permissions
steps.note: Users, groups, file modes, capabilities and process isolation are the primitives every container and server control is built from.

steps.label: HTTP
steps.note: The web attack surface is HTTP: methods, headers, cookies and status codes are where injection, session and access-control bugs are expressed.

steps.label: TCP/IP & the network stack
steps.note: Firewalls, segmentation, port scanning and traffic interception all assume you know what a connection is and where it can be observed.

steps.label: DNS
steps.note: DNS is both a dependency and an attack path — spoofing, subdomain takeover and exfiltration all live here, and every certificate is validated against a name.

steps.label: Cryptography basics
steps.note: Hashes, MACs, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, key derivation and randomness are the vocabulary of everything below; you need to know what each guarantees, not how to implement it.

steps.label: TLS
steps.note: TLS is where that theory becomes a handshake, a certificate chain and a trust store — and the place most 'secure transport' mistakes are made.

steps.label: HTTPS & certificate management
steps.note: Once TLS makes sense, the operational reality is issuance, rotation, expiry monitoring, HSTS and mixed content — the parts that break in production.

steps.label: Authentication
steps.note: Password storage, MFA, account recovery and session lifetime are the highest-leverage controls in most products, and the easiest to get subtly wrong.

steps.label: OAuth 2.0 & OIDC
steps.note: Delegated authorization is now the default for third-party and SSO access, so knowing the flows — and which ones are deprecated — prevents whole classes of token theft.

steps.label: JWT
steps.note: Signed tokens are everywhere and carry their own pitfalls: algorithm confusion, missing audience checks and the fact that a valid token cannot easily be withdrawn.

steps.label: RBAC & authorization models
steps.note: After proving who a caller is you must decide what they may do; broken access control is consistently the most common serious web vulnerability.

steps.label: OWASP Top 10 & web attacks
steps.note: Injection, XSS, SSRF, deserialization and access-control flaws are the concrete bugs the foundations above let you reason about — learn them as patterns, not as a checklist.

steps.label: CORS & browser security model
steps.note: Same-origin policy, CORS, CSP and cookie attributes are the browser-side controls that decide whether an injected script can actually do damage.

steps.label: Threat modelling
steps.note: Reviewing a design before it is built is far cheaper than finding the same flaw in a pen test, and it is the skill that turns an engineer into a security engineer.

steps.label: Rate limiting & abuse prevention
steps.note: Credential stuffing, scraping and enumeration are volume attacks, so limits, lockouts and anomaly detection are security controls rather than performance tuning.

steps.label: Secrets management
steps.note: Leaked credentials are a leading breach cause, so a vault, short-lived credentials and rotation must replace environment variables copied between machines.

steps.label: Container hardening
steps.note: Images inherit every vulnerability they package; minimal base images, non-root users, read-only filesystems and scanning are the baseline for anything you deploy.

steps.label: Kubernetes security
steps.note: A cluster multiplies blast radius: RBAC, network policies, admission control, service accounts and secret handling are what keep one compromised pod from owning everything.

steps.label: Supply chain & pipeline security
steps.note: The build system can deploy to production, which makes it a prime target — dependency pinning, provenance, signed artifacts and least-privilege runners belong here.

steps.label: Detection, logging & incident response
steps.note: Prevention always fails eventually, so audit logs, alerting on the right signals and a rehearsed response runbook decide whether an incident lasts hours or months.

steps.label: Design an authentication system
steps.note: Finish on a real design where identity, tokens, sessions, transport and revocation all interact — the place every topic above shows up at once.
